Euler and Fermat

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch three straight lines still pass through the same point.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the point names or the marked angles.
Look for the math

Build an equilateral triangle on each side of a triangle. Take the centres of those three triangles, and do it again on the other side: the two new triangles have the same centre. Something even stranger happens with the two Fermat points.

Two Fermat points and two Napoleon triangles

The outer equilateral triangles give A′B′C′ and the inner ones give a′b′c′; these are the two Napoleon triangles. Both are equilateral and both have the same centre as ABC: their centroid G, the average (A + B + C) / 3. The lines from each corner to the far tip of the equilateral triangle on the opposite side meet at a Fermat point. Turn the equilateral triangles the other way and the same construction gives the second one, F and f.

Ten Euler lines, one point

The Euler line of a triangle joins its centroid to its circumcenter. Choose any three of the five points A, B, C, F, f: there are ten ways. The page claims all ten Euler lines pass through G. The logic test checks every one of the ten on hundreds of triangles — the claim holds. This drawing shows the three lines for F, f and one corner (A, B or C); the page says the other seven are proved elsewhere.

The 120-degree turn

For the triangle CfF, call its centroid G′ and its circumcenter O. P is where B′C′ meets a′c′. A turn of 120° about G sends O exactly to P, so ∠OGP = 120° and O, G, a′, P lie on one circle; B′ lies on that circle too. The marked angles then match: ∠OGB′ = ∠Oa′B′ = ∠Pc′C′ = ∠fBA = ∠fF′A. They are equal as directed angles, so an ordinary angle may appear instead as its supplement — the test accepts either.

Why G is on the line

M is the midpoint of AB and m the midpoint of Ff. Both G and G′ divide their segments in the ratio 2 : 1, so GG′ ∥ Mm. The applet reflects F in M to make F′ (the page's text says f, a slip: the angles it quotes only work for F), and that gives Mm ∥ F′f. The angle chain above gives F′f ∥ GO. Put those together and G′, G, O are collinear — G lies on the Euler line of CfF. By the same argument it lies on the other two drawn lines.

Tick "Show special angles" and drag a corner: the marked angles change, but the three green lines keep crossing at G.
